> AGENT

Yes. The repo has a dedicated review pipeline under [dev/review/README.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/README.md:1).

It’s a three-stage process:

1. **Stage 1: Assess**
   One agent per open PR/issue reviews the item honestly and writes `dev/review/results/{pr|issue}-{number}.json`.

2. **Stage 2: Challenge**
   Accepted items get a devil’s advocate; rejected items get an angel’s advocate. Outputs go to separate `.stage2.json` files, plus `_cross-item.json` for duplicates, ordering, and interactions.

3. **Stage 3: Adjudicate + Execute**
   A final decision-maker reads both stages, verifies independently, presents decisions for approval, then cherry-picks/implements/rejects/defer items, tests after each, comments on GitHub, and records outcomes.

Key files:
- [dev/review/README.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/README.md:1)
- [dev/review/prompts/1-review-orchestrator.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/prompts/1-review-orchestrator.md:1)
- [dev/review/prompts/2-challenge-orchestrator.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/prompts/2-challenge-orchestrator.md:1)
- [dev/review/prompts/3-decide-and-execute.md](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/prompts/3-decide-and-execute.md:1)
- [dev/review/schema.json](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/review/schema.json:1)

There are also existing result files in `dev/review/results/`, so this process has been run before or is in progress.

The stated root cause is not correct: Bandit already excludes nested files under an absolute directory exclude because `_is_file_included` rejects paths where any excluded string is contained in the discovered filename; `bandit -r --exclude /tmp/project/.claude /tmp/project` skipped `/tmp/project/.claude/worktrees/bad.py` and scanned only the non-excluded file. Worse, this implementation expands all absolute path components, so an exclude like `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/.venv` adds `**/Users/**`, `**/Documents/**`, and `**/desloppify/**`, which can match the scan root and cause Bandit to scan zero files whenever exclude_dirs is non-empty. Because `collect_exclude_dirs` always emits default excludes, this risks silently disabling Python security detection for normal scans.\",\n+    \"reject_reason\": \"The underlying Bandit matching claim is false for the supported Bandit path, and the fix over-matches absolute path components enough to exclude the entire scan tree. First, `review --prepare --dimensions abstraction_fitness` goes through `do_prepare()` and `build_review_packet_payload()`, which writes `query.json` with `config` and `next_command` but no `prepared_packet_contract`; a following `review --run-batches` reaches `_load_or_prepare_packet()`, calls `_try_load_prepared_packet()` only when no explicit dimensions were passed, and rejects that prepared packet with `missing prepared packet contract metadata`, then rebuilds from args with no dimensions. Second, the Codex runner path writes prompt files but `_run_batch_task()` reads the full prompt text back into memory and passes it to `run_codex_batch()`, whose `codex_batch_command()` appends the prompt as a command-line argument. On Windows, `_resolve_executable()` may also wrap npm `.cmd` shims in `cmd /c`, and `_wrap_cmd_c()` collapses the entire invocation into one command string, so a large holistic prompt can plausibly exceed the Windows command-line length limit exactly as reported. This is worth fixing because it breaks targeted stale-dimension reviews and makes the automated Codex review path unusable on Windows for large packets.\",\n+    \"confidence\": \"high\",\n+    \"scope_estimate\": \"medium\",\n+    \"potential_duplicates\": [\n+      562\n+    ],\n+    \"real_problem\": true,\n+    \"suggested_fix\": \"Add `prepared_packet_contract` to packets produced by the prepare/external packet construction path so `--run-batches` can safely reuse `query.json` when the invocation contract matches. Add regression coverage for prepared single-dimension reuse and for Windows command construction not embedding a large prompt in the argv/cmd string.\"\n+  }\n+}\n*** End Patch\n"
}

The backtracking problem is real: the annotation sub-pattern `(?:@[\\\\w\\\\.\\\\(\\\\),<>\\\\s]+)\\\\s*` has overlapping whitespace consumption between the character class (which includes \\\\s) and the trailing \\\\s*, and wrapping in `()*` creates exponential backtracking on inputs with multiple @-prefixed tokens that don't ultimately match. Tested: 25 @-params causes the original regex to hang indefinitely while the possessive version completes in microseconds. Additionally, the possessive version actually fixes a latent correctness bug: the original regex would backtrack through annotations like @override and produce garbage single-character function names (e.g., 'd' instead of 'build' for `@override Widget build(...)`). The possessive version correctly captures the real function name in those cases. Requires Python >=3.11 which is already the project minimum.\",\n     \"confidence\": \"high\",\n     \"scope_estimate\": \"small\",\n     \"potential_duplicates\": []\n+  },\n+  \"stage3\": {\n+    \"decision\": \"IMPLEMENTED_ALREADY\",\n+    \"reasoning\": \"Accepted fix was already present in the integration branch as commit ab36319a. The Dart function declaration regex uses possessive quantifiers to avoid catastrophic backtracking while preserving normal annotation parsing.\",\n+    \"commit\": \"ab36319a\",\n+    \"changes_applied\": [\n+      \"Confirmed the Dart extractor regex already contains the accepted possessive-quantifier fix.\",\n+      \"Ran a focused sanity check for annotated method extraction and non-matching @-heavy input.\"\n+    ],\n+    \"tests\": [\n+      \"PYENV_VERSION=3.11.11 python - <<'PY' ... dart extractor regex sanity ... If agents return empty, partial, or rate-limit-shaped results, reduce the wave size and retry only failed batches. Launching 20+ subagents at once can exhaust API quota and produce no usable review output.\n+\n - Import first, fix after — import creates tracked state entries for correlation.\n - Target-matching scores trigger auto-reset to prevent gaming. Use the blind-review workflow described in your agent overlay doc (e.g. `docs/CLAUDE.md`, `docs/HERMES.md`).\n - Even moderate scores (60-80) dramatically improve overall health.\n*** End Patch\n"

{
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: /Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/docs/CODEX.md\n@@\n ### Subagent policy\n \n Do not ask Codex review or triage prompts to spawn their own child agents. The supported Codex path is the first-class batch runner above: it already isolates packet slices, supports parallel subprocess execution, preserves retry artifacts, and keeps execution guardrails outside the model prompt. Revisit this only after Codex exposes a stable non-interactive subagent contract that can cap concurrency, preserve blind-packet isolation, and retry failed child tasks without increasing cost or weakening guardrails.\n \n+### Sandbox\n+\n+Codex batch runs default to `-s workspace-write`. On hosts where that sandbox cannot run, such as WSL1 systems without the needed Linux namespace support, set `DESLOPPIFY_CODEX_SANDBOX=danger-full-access` in an externally sandboxed environment before running review batches. Supported values are `read-only`, `workspace-write`, and `danger-full-access`; invalid values fall back to `workspace-write`.\n+\n ### Triage workflow\n \n Prefer automated triage: `desloppify plan triage --run-stages --runner codex`\n*** End Patch\n"
}

{
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: README.md\n@@\n Scanning the parent directory that contains both will mix state and path context across unrelated codebases, producing unreliable results. Each `--path` target should be a single coherent project. Desloppify maintains separate state per language, so you can scan a TypeScript frontend and a Python backend from the same workspace without conflict — just target them individually.\n \n+## CI\n+\n+Desloppify works best in CI as a full-codebase health gate, not as a diff-only linter. Run the CI profile against the same coherent project path you scan locally:\n+\n+```bash\n+desloppify scan --path . --profile ci --no-badge\n+desloppify status --json\n+```\n+\n+`--profile ci` skips slow and subjective phases and bypasses the mid-cycle scan queue gate so a CI job can collect a fresh mechanical snapshot. Use `status --json` if you want a script to read the strict/objective scores and enforce your own threshold.\n+\n+Minimal GitHub Actions example:\n+\n+```yaml\n+name: desloppify\n+\n+on:\n+  pull_request:\n+  push:\n+    branches: [main]\n+\n+jobs:\n+  health:\n+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n+    steps:\n+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n+      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5\n+        with:\n+          python-version: \"3.11\"\n+      - run: pip install --upgrade \"desloppify[full]\"\n+      - run: desloppify scan --path . --profile ci --no-badge\n+      - run: desloppify status --json\n+```\n+\n+For monorepos, run one job or matrix entry per project path instead of scanning the workspace root. True incremental or diff-only scanning is not the supported model yet; compare full-codebase results across runs or enforce a project-level threshold.\n+\n ## How it works\n \n ```\n scan ──→ score ──→ review ──→ triage ──→ execute ──→ rescan\n*** End Patch\n"
}

> DEVELOPER

Are any of these bug fixes questionable? Like are anything where we're adding functionality or breaking functionality, or could be breaking functionality, or are they all fairly solid?

> AGENT

Mostly solid, but not all equal risk.

Low-risk / fairly solid:
- #581 non-finite numeric rejection: good fix, but I adjusted the PR approach to avoid `OverflowError` on huge ints.
- #602 Bash unused imports: good fix direction. I added the missing “only first argument after `source`/`.`” condition, which avoids a new false-positive class.
- #589 TS log cleanup else-chain preservation: low-risk because it prevents deleting empty `if` / `else if` blocks when followed by `else`. This may leave a few harmless empty branches behind, but avoids invalid output.

Medium-risk:
- #559 state repair recovery: useful and bounded, but inherently partial. It restores plan-backed skip decisions; it cannot recover deleted scan/score history if state and backup are gone.
- #565/#558 suppression fingerprints: valuable, but fingerprint matching can theoretically over-preserve a suppression if two findings have identical detector/name/summary/non-location details. I scoped it to exact suppressions and stable metadata, so risk is limited.
- #140 per-language scan/status: this adds functionality. It should not break normal `scan`/`status`, but `scan --by-language` can be slower and could expose language file-finder quirks in mixed repos. Aggregate is explicit equal-weight, which is defensible but not the only possible policy.

Potentially questionable / needs care:
- #529 R test coverage hooks: feature addition. Need verify the `strip_test_markers` behavior before accepting as-is.
- #539 persona rotation: prompt behavior feature, low runtime risk but subjective-output behavior changes.
- #573/#580 comment-aware brace scanning: these are the riskiest class because parser fallback state machines can regress strings/templates/comments. I haven’t implemented those yet in this resumed pass.
- #603 Rovo Dev: feature addition and depends on current external CLI shape. Needs current command verification before closing.

So: the completed issue fixes are reasonably solid, with the suppression and repair changes carrying normal compatibility risk. The PR batch still contains a few places where I’m intentionally not just merging blindly because the Stage 1 review found real conditional gaps.

{
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: /Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/dev/release-notes-drafts/v1.0.md\n+<p align=\"center\">\n+  <img src=\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/peteromallet/desloppify/main/assets/mascot-no-bg.png\" width=\"180\" alt=\"Desloppify mascot\">\n+</p>\n+\n+Desloppify 1.0 is a stability and agent-workflow release: broader runner support, better release-grade review/triage accounting, per-language score visibility, and a long tail of false-positive and state-recovery fixes from real-world dogfooding.\n+\n+---\n+\n+**241 files changed | 85 commits | release validation passing**\n+\n+## Headline Feature\n+\n+### First-Class Rovo Dev Runner\n+\n+Rovo Dev is now supported as both a review batch runner and a staged triage runner. You can run:\n+\n+```bash\n+desloppify review --run-batches --runner rovodev --parallel --scan-after-import\n+desloppify plan triage --run-stages --runner rovodev\n+```\n+\n+The native runner uses `acli rovodev run` subprocesses, preserves the same file-output/import shape as the Codex and OpenCode runners, and includes setup/update-skill support plus dedicated Rovo Dev docs. Thanks to **@awprice** for the original PR (#603).\n+\n+## Other Features\n+\n+### Per-Language Scorecards\n+\n+Mixed-language repositories can now inspect scan health by language instead of only seeing a single aggregate score. This makes it easier to separate, for example, a healthy Python package from a struggling TypeScript app inside the same repo. Closes #140.\n+\n+### Qwen-Code Skill Support\n+\n+Added Qwen-Code as a supported skill install target, with project and global skill detection matching the existing assistant integrations. Closes #532.\n+\n+### Review Persona Rotation\n+\n+Parallel review batches now rotate reviewer personas so large subjective reviews get a broader mix of perspectives instead of repeating the same framing across every batch. From PR #539 by **@gcascioe**.\n+\n+### R Language Improvements\n+\n+R support now includes Air formatter integration and stronger test coverage hooks, including broader assertion recognition for testthat-style tests. Thanks to **@sims1253** for the continued R work around PR #529.\n+\n+## Bug Fixes\n+\n+- **Prepared review packets are reused correctly** — batch runs no longer rebuild a different packet after `review --prepare --dimensions ...`, which also avoids Windows command-line length failures. Closes #541 and #562.\n+- **Codex sandbox override** — Codex review batches can override sandbox mode for constrained environments such as WSL1. Closes #534.\n+- **Review runner recovery** — batch failures, payload parsing, UTF-8 logs, and exception handling are more robust across runner backends.\n+- **Reflect ledger correctness** — colliding short issue tokens now require full IDs, repair prompts display unambiguous tokens, and observe-auto skips survive fresh reflect runs. PRs #584 and #585.\n+- **Comment-aware fallback scanners** — C#, C++, Dart, Rust, and TypeScript fallback scanners ignore braces/parens inside comments while preserving string/template handling. PRs #573 and #580.\n+- **TypeScript log cleanup** — removing debug logs no longer breaks `if` / `else if` / `else` chains. PR #589.\n+- **Bash source import detection** — the Bash unused-import detector now only treats `source` and `.` commands as imports. PR #602.\n+- **Non-finite score inputs** — review scoring rejects NaN/infinite floats while still handling huge integers safely. PR #581.\n+- **jscpd timeout cleanup** — timed-out duplicate-code scans now terminate the process group instead of leaving CPU-bound grandchildren behind. Closes #601.\n+- **Suppression durability** — file-path-prefixed suppressions survive common refactor/move scenarios. Closes #558 and #565.\n+- **State repair** — `plan repair-state` can recover more triage history after state loss. Closes #559.\n+- **Review item context** — bare review item IDs now recover summary/evidence context instead of surfacing opaque titles. Closes #566.\n+- **Rust detector false positives** — tightened Rust diagnostics, disabled generic Rust cycle/unused-import findings where Rust-specific semantics are required, and fixed async-locking/string-error edge cases. Closes #523, #543, #545, #549, #554, and #568.\n+- **CLI and queue UX** — detector lookup, scan-root validation, stale-finding reconciliation, skip/suppress attestation wording, queue progress, and cluster resolve behavior all received focused fixes.\n+\n+## Refactoring & Internal\n+\n+- Runner dispatch now has clearer backend seams so Codex, OpenCode, and Rovo Dev can share orchestration without hard-coding subprocess behavior.\n+- Reflect-stage accounting and disposition persistence have focused regression coverage for collision and observe-auto cases.\n+- Package data checks now cover bundled assistant docs and optional dependency metadata.\n+- The package metadata now marks Desloppify as `Production/Stable`.\n+\n+## Community\n+\n+Thank you to **@awprice** for the Rovo Dev runner, **@gcascioe** for review persona rotation, and **@sims1253** for the R language coverage work. Thanks also to the reporters behind the runner, Rust, TypeScript, state-repair, and constrained-host issues that shaped this 1.0 stabilization pass.\n*** End Patch\n"

tool_use exec_command
```json
{
  "cmd": "PYENV_VERSION=3.11.11 python - <<'PY'\nimport json\nimport subprocess\n\nrepo = \"peteromallet/desloppify\"\nrelease_url = \"https://github.com/peteromallet/desloppify/releases/tag/v1.0\"\nlabel = \"release:v1.0\"\n\ndef run(args, *, check=True):\n    result = subprocess.run(args, text=True, capture_output=True)\n    if check and result.returncode != 0:\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"{' '.join(args)}\\n{result.stderr or result.stdout}\")\n    return result.stdout.strip()\n\ndef gh_json(args):\n    out = run(args)\n    return json.loads(out) if out else []\n\nissues = gh_json([\n    \"gh\", \"issue\", \"list\", \"--repo\", repo, \"--label\", label,\n    \"--state\", \"all\", \"--limit\", \"200\", \"--json\", \"number,state\"\n])\nprs = gh_json([\n    \"gh\", \"pr\", \"list\", \"--repo\", repo, \"--label\", label,\n    \"--state\", \"all\", \"--limit\", \"200\", \"--json\", \"number,state\"\n])\n\nitems = [(item[\"number\"], \"issue\", item[\"state\"]) for item in issues]\nitems += [(item[\"number\"], \"pr\", item[\"state\"]) for item in prs]\nitems.sort(key=lambda item: item[0])\n\nposted = skipped = closed = 0\nfor number, kind, state in items:\n    comments = gh_json([\n        \"gh\", \"api\", f\"repos/{repo}/issues/{number}/comments\",\n        \"--jq\", \"[.[].body]\"\n    ])\n    if any(release_url in body for body in comments):\n        skipped += 1\n    else:\n        if kind == \"pr\":\n            body = (\n                \"Thanks for the contribution. This is included in v1.0: \"\n                f\"{release_url}\"\n            )\n        else:\n            body = (\n                \"Thanks for the report. This has shipped in v1.0, so the \"\n                f\"release decision is fixed/released: {release_url}\"\n            )\n        run([\"gh\", \"issue\", \"comment\", str(number), \"--repo\", repo, \"--body\", body])\n        posted += 1\n        print(f\"commented {kind} #{number}\")\n    if kind == \"issue\" and state.upper() == \"OPEN\":\n        run([\"gh\", \"issue\", \"close\", str(number), \"--repo\", repo, \"--comment\", f\"Closing now that v1.0 is released: {release_url}\"])\n        closed += 1\n        print(f\"closed issue #{number}\")\n\nprint(f\"release comments posted={posted} skipped_existing={skipped} closed={closed} total={len(items)}\")\nPY",

The core issue is GitHub attribution is commit-history based, not release-notes based. I found one release-note typo and I’m fixing that, but making GitHub’s contributor count reflect everyone requires preserving their commit authorship in the commits reachable from `v1.0`, or rewriting/rebuilding the release history to do so.

> AGENT

I’m going to do the low-risk correction immediately: update the published release body and the checked-in draft with the full PR contributor list and the corrected #539 author. That fixes human-visible attribution without rewriting the already-published tag.

> AGENT

GitHub’s contributor count is not driven by release-note prose. It is driven by commit metadata in the history reachable from the release tag.

What happened here: `v0.9.15..v1.0` only has one Git commit author locally:

```text
POM <[REDACTED]>
```

So GitHub does not see all those PR authors as commit contributors, even though their PRs were reviewed, accepted, labeled, commented, and included.

I corrected the low-risk part now:

- Fixed the wrong #539 attribution from `@gcascioe` to `@koshimazaki`.
- Added a full “PR Contributors” section to the published `v1.0` release.
- Committed/pushed that correction on `1.0.1`: `d2cf5c42 docs: correct v1.0 contributor attribution`.

For future releases, proper code attribution means one of these:

1. Merge the original PRs instead of manually reimplementing them, so GitHub preserves PR authorship.
2. Cherry-pick original PR commits with author metadata intact.
3. If squashing/reworking, add exact `Co-authored-by: Name <github-email>` trailers to the resulting commits. GitHub docs say co-authored commits are visible and can count when the email matches the user’s GitHub account.
4. Use GitHub’s generated release notes as a baseline, then layer the curated notes on top, so the PR contributor list is not missed.

For this already-published `v1.0`, the only way to make the GitHub contributor widget itself reflect everyone would be to rewrite/rebuild the `v1.0` git history and force-move `main`/`v1.0` to commits with preserved authors or co-author trailers. That is possible, but it is invasive now that the release is public. The safer correction is what I just did: fix the release body and make the attribution explicit.
